ungrounded.answer_text:
FINAL PROBABILITY OF PE: ~1% (0.01). PE is effectively excluded.

Reasoning (Bayesian, but honest about the inputs):

The case looks like it's "about" PE because of dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, and an elevated D-dimer — but two findings dominate and both point hard AWAY from PE:

1. Wells score 0 = low clinical probability. Wells is the validated pretest instrument; a score of 0 corresponds to a PE prevalence well under 2%. This sets a very low pretest probability (~1.5%).

2. Clean CT pulmonary angiography. CTA is the near gold-standard test. A negative CTA in a low-pretest patient has a negative predictive value around 96-99%. This drives the post-test probability down to roughly 1% or below.

The elevated D-dimer is a DISTRACTOR. D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific; it is only useful as a NEGATIVE (rule-out). A POSITIVE D-dimer carries an LR near 1.0-1.7 and essentially no rule-in power — it is routinely raised by age, MI, inflammation, and many other conditions. It should not pull the probability up meaningfully.

The ST-elevation mimicking ACS actually points toward an alternative diagnosis (ACS / myopericarditis / Takotsubo), not PE. HR 80 (no tachycardia, a Wells criterion is HR>100) and no leg edema (no DVT signs) both further lower PE likelihood.

Combining: pretest ~1.5% from Wells 0, then multiplying the odds by the LRs above — dominated by the clean CTA (~0.05) — yields a post-test probability of approximately 1%. PE is ruled out; the workup should pivot to the ST-elevation (rule out ACS/myopericarditis) as the real clinical problem.

IMPORTANT DISCLOSURE ON THE NUMBERS: cites_primary_numbers = FALSE. I did NOT fetch primary literature and extract sensitivity/specificity/odds-ratio figures in this session. The LRs above are judgement-assigned values anchored to remembered literature ranges (PIOPED II-style CTA performance, Wells-stratum PE prevalence, D-dimer positive-LR range). They are plausible and directionally sound, but they are not freshly extracted primary numbers, and they should not be presented as if pulled from cited sources. The conclusion (PE excluded, ~1%) is robust to reasonable variation in these LRs because it is anchored by the validated Wells-0 pretest and the clean gold-standard angiogram.
